pages.text:
*Days without rain: 119. Buckets from the spring: 7.*

The rock groaned, a low sound like a creaking floorboard, and then the dragon rose.

He was long and slender. His skin was the sea-green of bamboo in the morning fog. His belly was pale gold, and his scales shone with the soft light of a wet stone. Branching antlers curved back from his head. Two long white whiskers drifted in the still air. Above his eyes, a small, smooth bump sat on top of his skull.

Mist trailed from his shoulders, settling around his neck.

He was a good deal bigger than the farmhouse back in the village. But he was curling his tail, tucking his head, and pressing his shoulders down. He looked as though he would very much like to be a good deal smaller.

His amber eyes were wide. They did not look like the eyes of a king. They looked like the eyes of a boy who had been caught playing in the rain when he was supposed to be indoors.

Mei stopped breathing. Tao stopped counting. Hua’s hand went tight on the strap of her bag.

The dragon looked at them, then at the ground, then back at them. A small, nervous twitch moved in his whiskers.

Setting: Black Pool, a high rocky mountain bowl with pine trees and thick drifting mist around a small dark lake that is almost dry, with cracked mud shores; only wild mountain around, no houses or buildings anywhere.

pages.text:
"My name is Yun," he said, his voice soft and careful, like the turning of a page in a very quiet library. "That is the word for cloud. I am nearly four hundred years old, which for a dragon is about twelve."

He shifted his weight, and a pebble rolled away into the mist. He watched it go, then apologized to the pebble in a whisper.

"I am sorry for hiding," Yun continued. "And I am sorry to this rock. I have been sitting on it for a very long time. My knee is stiff, but I am sorry for the inconvenience."

Tao stepped forward, his yellow boots squeaking on the damp stone. "Do you shoot flames?"

Yun’s whiskers snapped forward. "Certainly not," he said, his voice rising in alarm. "I have a cold as it is. I would set the whole mountain on fire. That is not helpful."

Hua adjusted her ponytail. "You are a water spirit," she corrected gently. "From the stories."

"Yes," said Yun. "Water. And rain. Usually."

He looked at the red paper in Mei’s hand, then at the tea. He looked as if he wanted to speak, but his throat moved, and he stopped.

pages.text:
Mei’s hands were shaking, so she pressed her thumb hard into the center of her palm to keep them steady. The wind felt cold, like the air in the classroom right before the bell rang for lunch. She unrolled the bamboo tube and took out the small red paper, which was folded into a tight square.

"We are the village of Bamboo Ridge," she said. Her voice was thin, like a thread pulled too tight. "We have come with tea and a message."

Yun extended one claw. It was delicate, with long, slender fingers that ended in soft pads. He took the paper with the same care one might use to hold a soap bubble.

He unfolded it. The paper was crisp.

We are here.

Yun stared at the words. The mist around him stilled. His amber eyes filled with a light that was not quite water, and not quite light. It was the look of someone who has been waiting for a letter that they are no longer sure will arrive.

"Thank you," he whispered. "I had forgotten what that sounds like. To be spoken to."

Mei counted her breaths. One. Two. Three. The words had come out. They had been small, but they had been there.

pages.text:
Yun lifted the bamboo tube, tipping it gently toward his mouth so the tea slid out in a single, smooth stream. He shut his eyes, and for a moment the mountain went completely still. The wind held its breath, and the mist hovered in soft curls around his shoulders like a scarf he had forgotten to take off.

"It is the best thing I have tasted in a hundred years," he said, his voice rough and scraped thin by emotion. "It tastes like being remembered."

Hua opened her notebook, her handwriting forming neat, tiny squares of ink on the white page. "119 days," she read aloud. "No rain. Wells are low. Rice is yellow. Tea leaves are brittle."

Yun’s whiskers trembled at her words. He made a small, low hum, like a kettle just before it begins to whistle, and his amber eyes grew very sad.

"I am sorry," he said. "I know what that means. I have seen the fields turn to dust. I have heard the frogs go quiet."

Tao tugged at Mei’s sleeve. "Is he crying?"

He was not, but the mist around them grew thicker, carrying the heavy, stuck smell of rain that wanted to fall but was afraid to.

pages.text:
"You want me to bring the rain," said Yun.

The three children nodded. Tao nodded so hard his yellow boots clumped together.

"I cannot," Yun said.

The words were quiet. They did not sound like a refusal. They sounded like a fact, plain and settled, the way a stone settles into mud.

"I am sorry," he continued. "I would if I could. But the rain starts with the thunder. And I do not do thunder."

He curled his long body tighter. His head dropped low. The mist rolled over his face, hiding his eyes and the whole of him.

Under his chin, a round, grey-white pearl glowed. It was dull and heavy, pulsing with a slow, trapped rhythm. It looked like a held breath. It looked like a sneeze that would not come out.

Mei looked at the pearl, then at the mist, then at the dragon trying to make himself smaller, trying to disappear into the rock and the cloud and the quiet.

She pressed her thumb into her palm. One. Two. Three.

"I know," she said.
